newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close lower as tightening fears rise.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close lower as tightening fears rise.

text.p: The prices of U.S. government securities closed sharply lower Friday following stronger-than-expected economic news that heightened expectations of further monetary policy tightening.

The Labor Department reported that producer prices fell 0.1 percent, but excluding the volatile food and energy components, rose 0.4 percent. In addition, retail sales rose 0.2 percent in March, but January and February sales figures were revised upward, February's by nearly double in a series in which revisions often outweigh the headline number.

Maureen Mooney, senior analyst at GovPX, said trading activity in the hour after the release of PPI amounted to $20.7 billion, a record amount following a PPI release. By noon, volume in two-year notes was $7.0 billion versus the $2.8 billion recent average on Fridays, she said.

Analysts said they expected key levels of 7.0 percent on the 10-year and 7.25 percent on the 30-year bond could be expected to be tested in coming sessions as anticipation grew that the Federal Reserve would again tighten monetary policy at its May meeting. Others said such fears were unwarranted as the market already had priced in another rate hike.

"There is clearly a negative sense in the market. But we may have already made an allowance for more nasty numbers next week, particularly CPI," said Anthony Karadakis, senior financial economist at First National Bank of Chicago. "Today we made new lows."
Karadakis was referring to yields that ended at 7.17 percent on the long bond, the highest since the 7.18 percent seen at the close on July 8 of last year.
"Nobody wants to try to catch a falling knife. You don't want to get in the way of this thing (a falling market)," Karadakis said.

He said a busy economic calendar next week may help participants decide whether the Federal Reserve would tighten again in May and, if so, a full adjustment to that had already been priced into prices.

"(A yield of) 7.25 percent is what everybody is talking about, but I never put a lot of weight on any one number. It's the economic numbers that affect psychology," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp. "The numbers we saw today were very disappointing."
Johnson warned that a CPI reading of 0.4 percent or higher could be very troubling to the bond market next week.

A reading of 0.4 percent or higher would push yields on the 30-year issue to 7.25 percent or above very quickly, Johnson said. Economists polled by Reuter expected, on average, to see a rise 0.2 percent in CPI.
Johnson said the next major number was the Employment Cost Index, due April 29, though the Philadelphia Fed's survey and durable goods could rattle the market before that.
The ECI, especially the benefits component, will be crucial, Johnson said. "But the discounting may be over and we'll come back again on Monday to establish new ranges," he said.
The Federal Reserve refrained from entering the banking system during its usual midmorning intervention period Friday.

The Treasury's 30-year bond closed off 21/32 at 93-11/32 to yield 7.17 percent. The 10-year note closed down 13/32 at 94-30/32, yielding 6.97 percent. The five-year note traded off 9/32 at 99-3/32 to yield 6.84 percent. The two-year note closed down 3/32 at 99-18/32, yielding 6.49 percent.
The three-month bill ended up two basis points at 5.16 percent; the six-month bill was up three basis points at 5.41 percent and the year bill was up four basis points at 5.68 percent.
